The Memory layer stores stable facts such as user preferences and environment configuration, using key-value or document form, auto-loaded at session start. The Skill layer stores standard operating procedures and best practices, using structured document form, actively loaded on demand by the agent. The Session Search layer uses FTS full-text indexing to store complete conversation history, supporting keyword search and LLM summarization. The key benefit of three-layer separation is that each layer's storage format, loading strategy, and update frequency can be optimized independently, avoiding the systemic inefficiency of using a single mechanism to handle all types of knowledge.

1uxj9hp:278: Hermes introduces regex-based threat pattern recognition at the memory write layer—a pragmatic but limited security measure. The pragmatism lies in blocking the most common prompt injection patterns at extremely low computational cost, without needing complex NLP models for semantic analysis. The limitation is that regex cannot defend against semantic-level injection attacks (e.g., bypassing pattern matching through natural language descriptions). This suggests that for self-improving systems, prompt injection defense requires multi-layer strategies—input layer (regex/rule filtering), reasoning layer (having the model judge content reasonableness before writing), and audit layer (post-hoc inspection of recorded content). Currently, most agent frameworks implement only the first layer, which is insufficient in highly adversarial scenarios.
1v95gpm:306: Hermes chooses to design dedicated tools for the skill mechanism (skill_list/skill_view/skill_manage) rather than using generic read/write tools to manipulate skill files—a design decision with deep engineering-philosophy considerations. Generic tools offer greater flexibility (one tool can handle all operations), but they increase the cognitive burden and error rate of model invocation; dedicated tools are less flexible but make the model's tool selection clearer and less error-prone. This reflects a core tension in agent system design: how to balance "tool specialization" against "tool unification." Hermes's answer is: for high-frequency, standardized operations (such as skill management), dedicated tools are superior to generic ones; for low-frequency, creative operations (such as arbitrary file editing), generic tools are more appropriate.

53qvbk:1660: ] The Agent actively saves memory in the following situations: user corrections — "remember this" / "don't do that again"; user preferences — name, role, timezone, coding style, communication habits; environment discoveries — OS, installed tools, project structure, API versions; convention learning — project-specific norms, tool quirks, workflows; stable facts — information still useful in future sessions. Session Search: learning from raw conversations. Memory stores conclusions, Skill stores methods, but real learning often happens during trial and error. Those failed attempts, wrong assumptions, and sudden insights do not automatically become Memory or Skill, yet they contain valuable experience. Suppose the user asks: "How did we fix that bug last time?" Memory might record "the user uses Python 3.9"; Skill might record "the general bug-fixing process". But the actual line of code that solved the problem, the key error message, and the order of trial-and-error attempts exist only in the raw conversation. The concrete session search technical scheme is as follows: • FTS5 full-text index: all messages are indexed in real time into an SQLite FTS5 virtual table • Relevance ranking: sorted by keyword match score • Session grouping: take the most relevant few sessions • LLM summarization: use a cheap model (e.g., Gemini Flash) to generate a summary with metadata • Return result: instead of returning the full raw conversation record, return an LLM-generated summary containing the complete thread of "problem → attempted process → final solution". Memory, skills, and sessions all store past experience. Memory is "passive recall"—loaded automatically in every session; the Agent knows it without needing to call a tool. Skill is "active loading + self-maintenance"—the Agent needs to call skill_view to read details, and can also use skill_manage to create new skills or fix outdated ones. Session Search is "on-demand recall"—it only searches when the user mentions past conversations, and is not resident in context. The comparison among the three is as follows: mechanism | stored content | usage | role in Self-Improving. Memory: stable facts (user preferences, environment info); automatically injected into System Prompt each session; added/modified proactively through the memory tool; avoids repeatedly asking for already-confirmed information. Skill: procedural knowledge (operation steps, best practices); index (name + description) shown in System Prompt, full content loaded on demand via skill_view; created/modified/deleted via skill_manage; avoids re-inventing verified processes. Session Search: raw conversation history (complete thought trajectories); proactively searches keywords via the session_search tool, LLM generates structured summaries; avoids repeating mistakes and stepping on already-hit pitfalls. A complete self-improve workflow is as follows, achieving a higher starting point for the next task than the previous one: • Step 1: the user asks "help me summarize this week's HN headlines and send them to Telegram" • Step 2: the Agent starts the session; the system prompt automatically includes USER.md ("User prefers short summaries") and the Skills index (discovers the "weekly-digest" skill is relevant) • Step 3: the Agent calls skill_view("weekly-digest") to load the skill and executes it step by step • Step 4: during execution, it finds the skill's "RSS scraping" is outdated; the user actually uses the HN API. The Agent calls skill_manage(action='patch') to update the skill • Step 5: the user says "only 5 headlines from now on". The Agent calls memory(action='add', target='user', content='User wants HN digest capped at 5 headlines') • Step 6: the disk is updated, but this session's system prompt remains unchanged • Step 7: the next week the user asks the same question. At startup, the system prompt already contains the new memory and the patched skill. The user does not need to repeat "only 5" or correct the skill error.
